title: Daniel's Seventy Sevens
lead: In Daniel 9:24-27 the angel Gabriel tells Daniel that 'seventy sevens' (usually read as seventy periods of seven years, 490 years) have been marked off for his people and city. The passage counts seven sevens, sixty-two sevens and one seven, names two 'anointed' figures, and ends with a covenant, an end to sacrifice and a desolator. No other passage of the Bible has been read in so many ways, by Jews, Catholics, Orthodox, Protestants, Adventists and others. This page sets the readings side by side on the same questions.

sections.h: The same questions for every reading
sections.b: Every reading answers these: Where does the count start (the 'word' of 9:25)? What is a 'seven' (a week of days, seven years of 360 days or of 365, or a symbolic number)? Who is 'an anointed one, a ruler' (9:25) and who is the 'anointed one' cut off (9:26)? Who is 'the ruler who is to come' and who is 'he' of 9:27? Is there a gap between the sixty-ninth and seventieth seven? What happens to the temple? The Masoretic Text puts its main pause after 'seven sevens' in 9:25; Theodotion and the Latin Vulgate join the seven and the sixty-two, and the Old Greek counts and orders the whole passage differently (see the variants and the note at Daniel 9:25).

The critical majority since the 19th century (Montgomery, Collins and many Catholic and Protestant scholars). Jeremiah's seventy years become seventy sevens of years, from the fall of Jerusalem (587/586 BC) to the persecution under Antiochus IV. Seven sevens (49 years) reach Cyrus or the high priest Jeshua (538 BC); sixty-two sevens run to the murder of the high priest Onias III (171 BC, 2 Maccabees 4:33-38); the last seven is 171-164 BC, with the sacrifice stopped in its middle (167 BC, 1 Maccabees 1:54). The covenant with 'the many' is the Hellenizers' covenant with the nations (1 Maccabees 1:11-15). The count is schematic: 490 years from 587 BC reach 97 BC, not 164 BC, and the author may have known the exile's length only roughly.

The 490 years reach Christ. Julius Africanus (reported by Eusebius, Proof of the Gospel 8.2) counted from Artaxerxes' twentieth year (445/444 BC); Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Eusebius, Augustine (City of God 18.34) and Jerome (who records several counts) took the sevens to Christ. Hippolytus of Rome (about AD 200) is an early witness to a gap: he takes the sixty-nine sevens to Christ's coming and puts the last seven at the end of the age, with Antichrist, Elijah and Enoch, divided at its midpoint by the abomination of desolation (On Christ and Antichrist 43, 47, 64). Calvin ends them at Christ's death and the destruction of Jerusalem. Modern defenders include Hengstenberg, E. J. Young (who reads the sevens as symbolic), Baldwin, Kline and Archer. The anointed one cut off is Christ; he 'confirms a covenant' in the last seven and ends sacrifice by his death (Hebrews 9-10); the city and sanctuary fall in AD 70. Starting points: 458/457 BC (Ezra 7), 445/444 BC (Nehemiah 2) or 538 BC (Cyrus).

sections.b: The 70 sevens are 'cut off' from the 2,300 evenings and mornings of Daniel 8:14; both begin with the decree of Artaxerxes in 457 BC. Sixty-nine sevens reach AD 27, Christ's baptism (the 'anointed one'); he is cut off in the middle of the seventieth seven (AD 31), and the 70 sevens end in AD 34. The 2,300 'days' (years) then end in 1844 with the cleansing of the sanctuary (Fundamental Belief 24). Critics inside the church, such as Desmond Ford (1980), disputed the link between the two periods.

The sixty-nine sevens run from 455 BC (the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, Nehemiah 2:1) to AD 29, Jesus' baptism and anointing as Messiah. The seventieth seven ends in AD 36 with the first Gentile converts (Insight on the Scriptures).

Associated with Robert Anderson (The Coming Prince, 1881), the Scofield Reference Bible, Walvoord, Pentecost and Hoehner. Sixty-nine sevens of 360-day years (483 years, or 173,880 days) run from the decree of 445/444 BC to Christ's entry into Jerusalem (Anderson: AD 32; Hoehner dates the cross to AD 33). A gap, the church age, follows (the idea of a gap before the last seven is older than Anderson: Hippolytus put the seventieth seven at the end of the age); the seventieth seven is a future seven-year tribulation. 'The people of the coming ruler' (the Romans) destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70, but the 'ruler to come' is the Antichrist, who makes a covenant with the many (Israel), breaks it in the middle (9:27) and sets up the abomination (Matthew 24:15; 2 Thessalonians 2:4). Critics, including other premillennialists, dispute the gap and the change of subject.

Historicist (Protestant from the Reformation into the 19th century; Joseph Mede, Isaac Newton): the 490 years end in the first century, and the day-year principle governs the other prophetic periods of Daniel and Revelation. Preterist (the name is modern; Moses Stuart, Kenneth Gentry): everything in 9:24-27 was fulfilled in the first century, in the ministry of Jesus (confirming the covenant for half a seven) and the war of AD 66-70.

The Reformation confessions that name the pope as the Antichrist (Westminster Confession 25.6; Second London Confession 26.4) and the Catholic counter-readings that answered them (Ribera and Bellarmine, futurist; Alcazar, preterist) belong to the little-horn readings of Daniel 7, 8 and 11, which the parts on those chapters set out; they are not quoted here as readings of the seventy sevens.

Medieval Jewish commentators disagree among themselves, and the page quotes only the three it can show. Seder Olam Rabbah 28 (read on Sefaria) gives 70 years for the destruction and 420 for the Second Temple's building. Rashi (on Sefaria) adds 70 years of exile to 420 to make 490, from the first destruction to the second; the 'anointed king' of 9:25 is Cyrus, the 'anointed' of 9:26 is Agrippa, and the 'coming ruler' is Titus. Ibn Ezra (on Sefaria) counts the seven sevens to the coming of Nehemiah and the sixty-two as the years of the Second Temple; he rejects Saadia Gaon's reckoning of 490 years to the destruction and argues that the half-week is 1,290 days. The Talmud discourages calculation (Sanhedrin 97b: 'May the bones of those who calculate the end rot').

This page gives no count for Ramban or Abravanel, because their texts were not read for it.

Seven times seventy is a figure of fullness and not a calendar: 70 x 7 echoes Leviticus 25-26 (seventy sabbatical cycles of the land's rest) and the seventy years of Jeremiah. Held by older and modern conservative scholars (Young; Kline in a messianic form).

The Melchizedek scroll (11Q13) arranges history in ten jubilees (490 years), and uses 'an anointed prince' from Daniel 9:25 for an end-time figure, as reported by its editors. The jubilee frame (Leviticus 25:8-12) is a link between the 490 years and the release of the land.

sections.h: Reading the passage with the prayer
sections.b: The seventy sevens are the answer to a prayer, not a free-standing timetable. Gabriel comes 'at the time of the evening offering' while Daniel confesses the curse of the law (9:11-13), and the six goals of 9:24 (end of rebellion, sin, wrongdoing; lasting righteousness; vision and prophet sealed; a most holy place anointed) answer that confession. Whatever the count, the passage says that Jerusalem's trouble will end after a long and fixed course.
